That is the end of Part 4. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers.

part.title: Urban heat islands

turns.text: Good morning, everyone. Today we're moving on from transportation to something that affects almost every city on this continent, and that's what's known as the urban heat island. Put simply, it's the way built-up areas end up noticeably warmer than the countryside around them.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: On a summer day, a downtown core can be several degrees hotter than nearby farmland. Now, most people assume the difference is biggest in the middle of the afternoon, when the sun's at its strongest. In fact, that's not really the case. The gap between city and countryside is usually widest at night, because the city keeps releasing the heat it stored up during the day, while rural areas cool down fast.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: So why does this happen? Well, the first reason is the materials we build with. Brick and concrete both soak up heat, but the real culprit is asphalt, the dark material on our roads and parking lots. On a sunny afternoon, it can get hot enough to burn your hand.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: The second reason is the lack of vegetation. Plants draw water up from the soil and release it through their leaves, and as that water turns to vapor, it takes heat out of the air. This process, evaporation, is basically nature's air conditioning. Replace a meadow with a shopping mall, and you lose it.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Third, there's the shape of the city itself. When tall buildings line narrow streets, you get what planners call canyons. Sunlight bounces from wall to wall instead of escaping, and the wind can't get through to carry the warm air away.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: And finally, there's waste heat from cars, from factories, and, rather ironically, from air conditioners pumping hot air out onto the street. So that's four causes, all working together.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Okay, so what are the effects? Let's start with health. Heat waves are one of the deadliest kinds of extreme weather in North America, and the people most at risk aren't always the ones you'd expect.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Young children are vulnerable, yes, but the biggest danger is to older people who live alone, often in top-floor apartments, with nobody checking on them. Many of them don't realize how dangerous the heat is until it's too late.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Heat also makes air quality worse. Higher temperatures speed up the chemical reactions that produce ground-level ozone, which irritates the lungs and is especially bad for people with asthma. So on the hottest days, the air is also at its most harmful to breathe.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Then there's energy. When it's hot, everybody turns up the air conditioning at the same time, usually between about four and, well, seven in the evening. Electricity bills go up, of course, but the bigger worry is the power grid. If demand gets too high, the utilities simply can't keep up, and that's when you see blackouts, which switch off the very air conditioning that vulnerable people depend on.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Right. So what can cities do about all this? The most obvious answer is trees. A mature tree shades the ground and cools the air through its leaves, as we discussed.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: But where you plant it really matters. A lot of homeowners think the south side of a building is best. Actually, research shows the biggest savings come from trees on the west side, because they block the low, intense sun of late afternoon. That's exactly when buildings are at their hottest.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: The challenge is that city streets aren't a great place for a tree to grow. Under the sidewalk, the soil is packed hard and full of pipes and cables, so there's very little room for roots to spread. That's why so many street trees die young, and why some cities now build special underground frames that hold loose soil beneath the pavement.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: The second solution is what we call cool roofs. A normal dark roof can reach over 150 degrees Fahrenheit in summer. A cool roof is covered with a reflective coating, usually white, that sends most of the sunlight straight back into the sky. New York, for example, has had volunteers treating thousands of rooftops this way.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Cool roofs can go on almost any building, but they're cheapest and simplest on flat roofs, the kind you see on warehouses, schools and apartment blocks. On a steep roof, the work's harder and more dangerous. And frankly, a lot of homeowners just don't like the look of a bright white roof on their house.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: There is one drawback, though. In places with cold winters, like Chicago or Toronto, a cool roof reflects away sunlight you'd actually like to have in January. So your heating costs can go up slightly in the colder months. In most cases, though, the summer savings are far bigger than that winter penalty.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Okay, I'll stop there for today. For next week, I'd like you to look at a map of your own neighborhood and think about where the hottest spots might be, and which of these solutions would suit them. We'll compare notes in the seminar.
turns.speaker: lecturer

questions.evidence: A cool roof is covered with a reflective coating

explanation.en: A cool roof is covered with a reflective coating, usually white, which sends sunlight back into the sky.
explanation.ru: На «холодную крышу» ("cool roof") наносят отражающее покрытие ("reflective coating"), обычно белое, которое отправляет солнечный свет обратно в небо.
explanation.uk: На «холодний дах» ("cool roof") наносять відбивне покриття ("reflective coating"), зазвичай біле, яке відправляє сонячне світло назад у небо.
